item.title: Wireless Android Auto solved one problem for me, and then created 3 more
item.itunes:title: Wireless Android Auto solved one problem for me, and then created 3 more
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I generally prioritize wireless connectivity over wired options for convenience. Between Ethernet and Wi-Fi, I would choose Wi-Fi for my laptop because, frankly speaking, it's a portable device meant to be carried around the house, and a wired connection just ties it down. However, when it comes to Android Auto, or even CarPlay for that matter, I would go with a cable every time, and I have my reasons for that.

It's not like I haven't tried wireless Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. I have for a few months, and it did solve the cable problem. Still, I've realized wired is simply better for me. It may not be for everyone or in every situation, but the problems I faced with wireless Android Auto were, simply put, a deal-breaker. A few months later, with wireless Android Auto and CarPlay, I realized that fixing the cable problem isn't a good enough reason to give up what actually matters.

Battery life took a hit

Wireless connectivity takes a toll on the battery

The first thing I noticed after switching to wireless Android Auto was that my phone's battery didn't last as long. That's expected, since your phone isn't being charged at the same time, and it may not be a big problem for many. But with a three-year-old phone, the impact was more significant than I initially anticipated. And it was something I wasn't willing to compromise on.

I know you could connect your phone to the 12V lighter socket and get faster charging, but that negates the very purpose of wireless connectivity. Your phone is still hooked up with a cable. Personally, that trickle charge from the Android Auto/Apple CarPlay-compatible port doesn't bother me. My phone's battery level is always higher when I step out of the car than when I step in, and it's all that matters.

This $30 accessory changed how I charge my phone in my car while using Android Auto

This 12V 130W USB-C and USB-A adapter is exactly what my card needed.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

The occasional lag

Wired is generally more reliable

Despite being in such close quarters, the wireless connection between the car's head unit and my phone wasn't always seamless. I experienced lag on a couple of occasions. I never experienced that when my phone was connected by cable. And it wasn't just the occasional lag. Sometimes the system froze for a couple of seconds when I tapped the screen too many times in quick succession.

You can overlook this part on a short city drive, but on highways, when you are cruising at higher speeds, you want the system to be lag-free and responsive. Wired Android Auto and CarPlay have consistently delivered that for me, and there were times I actually regretted switching to a wireless connection. Thankfully, I had a cable most of the time, so whenever the connection acted up, I hooked my phone up to it.

Overheating issues

My biggest concern

This was perhaps my biggest problem with the wireless setup, both on CarPlay and Android Auto. Honestly, I can deal with battery drain and the occasional lag, but not overheating. Because when your phone overheats, performance takes a hit, and it eventually affects the wireless connection. Again, it's understandable for a phone to overheat, especially one that's fairly old, since it actively uses both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, but for me, it's happened far too often.

I guess it may also have to do with where I live. It's hot here for most of the year. I eventually found a workaround — keeping my phone in a cupholder with an AC vent right behind it — but it wasn't ideal. Once you lose portability, there's really no point in going wireless, whether it's Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. And given the other problems I faced (as discussed later), wired Android Auto made more sense.

Wireless Android Auto isn't for everyone

Yet it's a better choice for some

I have tried it, and I have come to the conclusion that wireless Android Auto doesn't suit everyone. It's not just me. If you look at the forums, you will see these are common concerns. And it's not that Android Auto or Apple CarPlay are badly designed. In many cases, it's the car's head unit to blame. Sometimes, it's your phone. Or, if you are using an adapter to add wireless capabilities to your car, that could be the culprit, too. For me, moving back to the cable, something I wanted to get rid of, fixed things.

That said, I also know that the system works flawlessly for others. There may be some occasional hiccups, but for the most part, wireless Android Auto works as well as the wired connection, or sometimes even better. And let's be honest, there's no denying the fact that it's a lot more convenient. Having the phone hooked to your car via a cable isn't the most pleasant experience, but it's a price I have to pay for a stable connection, longer battery life, and to avoid overheating.

I switched back to wired Android Auto and CarPlay, and I don't miss wireless for one key reason

A wired connection is generally more reliable, more so when you are using an external adapter

8
By  Kazim Alvi

I ultimately switched back to a wired connection

I went back to the cable because I had to, but if wireless Android Auto works well for you, there's no reason you can't do the same. It all comes down to preferences and personal experience. But I also want to highlight a couple of things I noticed that could be seen as downsides.

On wireless Android Auto, the audio quality wasn't as good. Of course, an average user may not notice the difference, but some people can. Also, when my spouse and I got into the car together, the head unit would sometimes connect to her phone instead of mine (and vice versa), since both were paired, and we would have to spend the next minute fixing it.

Frankly, these aren't major annoyances, and I can happily live with them. But the three that I did face were deal-breakers, things that ultimately made the cable feel like a valuable addition to the setup and not a problem that I thought it was.

item.title: I integrated Proxmox with Home Assistant, and my home lab manages itself now
item.itunes:title: I integrated Proxmox with Home Assistant, and my home lab manages itself now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you’re as fond of Proxmox as I am, you’re probably aware that there are several ways to control your workstations besides its powerful web UI. For example, the shell interface on the host is pretty effective for tackling hardcore PCI passthrough, file transfer, ZFS pool manipulation, and other advanced tasks, while the Proxmox Datacenter Manager offers a more unified control UI when you’ve got multiple standalone and clustered PVE nodes in your arsenal. And that’s before you include third-party management utilities like ProxMenuX that you can configure directly on your Proxmox server.

However, the most unhinged management tool I use for my Proxmox-heavy home lab is Home Assistant. Of course, HASS is primarily a smart home platform, but thanks to the talented Home Assistant community, you can pair it with just about any non-IoT product, including the likes of Proxmox.

I turned a nearly 10-year-old laptop into the most useful machine in my home lab

I can't imagine my home lab without it

2
By  Ayush Pande

The unofficial PVE integration lets me pair Proxmox nodes with Home Assistant

This integration lets Home Assistant pull practically every Proxmox stat as an entity

Although Home Assistant has tons of useful integrations baked in, the one I used for this project doesn’t ship with the platform and needs to be configured manually. Specifically, I’m talking about the ProxmoxVE integration by genius developer dougiteixeira, which can read practically every aspect of my home servers. And I’m not just talking about the resource consumption metrics, uptime, or other monitoring-centric stats that the likes of Pulse can grab, either.

Rather, Home Assistant pulls the controls for every virtual guest, storage pool, and even the underlying host as entities, essentially recognizing my Proxmox infrastructure as any ol’ smart gizmo. As such, I can toss my Proxmox LXCs into a dashboard and power them on, schedule backups, and turn them off using simple actions without so much as heading to the PVE web UI. My home lab includes a couple of independent Proxmox workstations alongside a 2-node (+1 Raspberry Pi Q-device) in a ZFS replication environment, and this integration works with every single system.

I’ve got a smartphone and a tablet configured as smart panels for different rooms, and with a little bit of dashboard beautification via the Bubble Card integration, I can easily control my essential VMs and LXCs using a single tap. I’ve even exposed a handful of virtual guests to my Home Agent-powered conversation model, and as long as I don’t butcher the pronunciation of my LXCs or VMs, I can use voice commands to manage them.

Of course, the ProxmoxVE integration disables many of the power cycle, backup, and failover management actions to prevent misconfigured HASS setups from breaking home servers. But since I manage everything in a controlled environment, I’ve enabled most of these controls.

Toss in some smart devices, and you can build wild Proxmox automation pipelines

My trigger-action rules involve both smart gizmos and Proxmox systems

Automations are a crucial part of Home Assistant’s smart home management prowess, but since my PVE nodes add more entities to HASS, I can freely use them for my trigger-action chains. I’ve got a couple of LXCs that rely on each other, and I’ve created automation workflows that automatically boot the closely-knit containers whenever I power on one of them. My Paperless-ngx setup involving Paperless AI and Paperless-GPT is one such example, and I’ve also got a few VM backup snapshot tasks configured for simple triggers.

The best part? My entire smart home arsenal is connected to Home Assistant, and this includes the smart plugs powering my Proxmox nodes. So, I can not only monitor their power consumption, but also use these statistics to control their virtual guests. For example, my backwater town has blackouts every once in a while. Rather than constantly scurrying around the house trying to manually power down everything when the power goes out, I’ve created a simple automation pipeline where HASS gracefully shuts down my PVE nodes when the UPS backup sinks below the 40% mark.

Likewise, if my UPS reports excessive power consumption on a PVE node, Home Assistant notifies me about the virtual guest that’s hogging a lot of system resources. Heck, there’s even room for some wacky automation chains. A smart toothbrush that sends shutdown signals to non-essential LXCs and VMs every time I brush my teeth at night is just as fun (and practical) as it sounds. I’m also tempted to pair a vibration sensor with my ESP32 and have it power on certain Proxmox virtual guests every time I hit my desk. The possibilities are endless.

6 of the coolest HACS integrations for Home Assistant users

Level up your Home Assistant game with these neat HACS integrations

3
By  Ayush Pande

I’ve even added my NAS to Home Assistant

Besides my Proxmox workstations, I’ve also added TrueNAS metrics to Home Assistant using a different integration. That way, I can monitor my storage servers and virtualization workstations from their own dashboards, and even build cool PVE automations involving stats from my NAS.

That said, I’ll admit that I’ve disabled a lot of entities for my NAS on Home Assistant. Unlike my easy-to-restore virtual guests, I wouldn’t want to disrupt the backup tasks for my NAS. Or worse, accidentally render it offline in the middle of a transfer task.

item.title: I use these 5 open-source tools to improve my development workflow on Windows
item.itunes:title: I use these 5 open-source tools to improve my development workflow on Windows
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows has been my main development environment for years, and I’ve learned that productivity often comes down to the small things. A few extra clicks here, a repetitive task there, or a tool that makes me work harder than necessary can quickly add up. I started looking beyond the usual software recommendations and tried some open-source projects instead. What surprised me was how many fit naturally into how I already work. They didn't require me to completely change my setup or learn complicated workflows. Instead, they solved everyday annoyances and made my development environment feel more practical.

WinGet

Software installation without the hassle

Instead of opening a browser, searching for an application, downloading its installer, and clicking through the setup process, I can install many of the tools I need directly from the terminal. A simple command is usually enough to install an application.

What I like most is how useful it becomes when setting up a new Windows machine. I can quickly install several applications without manually visiting their websites one by one. It also makes updating installed applications much easier, since I can check for available updates and upgrade them from the same place.

I also use WinGet to quickly check whether a particular application is available before installing it. It has made software installation feel less like a separate task and more like a normal part of my development workflow.

Espanso

Less repetitive typing

I didn't realize how often I was typing the same things until I started looking for a way to avoid it. Code snippets, commands, email addresses, URLs, and other small pieces of text kept showing up in my daily work, and typing them manually felt like unnecessary effort.

Espanso lets me replace those repetitive inputs with short keywords. I can type a few characters and have them automatically expand into longer text. This is especially useful for commands or snippets I use frequently, since I don't have to keep searching for them or type them from scratch.

Another thing I like is that it works across Windows applications. I can use the same shortcuts in my editor, terminal, browser, or other tools instead of setting them up separately for each application.

I also keep my frequently used snippets organized in its configuration files, making them easy to update when something changes. It's become a simple way to cut repetitive typing from my development routine.

Zed

Less clutter, faster coding

I wanted a code editor that felt quick and responsive, especially when I was switching between files or working on smaller projects. That is where Zed caught my attention. It starts quickly, feels lightweight, and doesn't make me wait around when I just want to open a file and start working.

The interface is also clean without feeling stripped down. I can keep my project files, code, and terminal within the same workspace without the editor getting in my way. Switching between files feels smooth, and I like how little visual clutter there is while I'm coding.

Zed also handles the everyday things I expect from a modern editor, including syntax highlighting, code navigation, and Git integration. I don't need much time configuring it before I'm productive.

It hasn't replaced every editor I use, but for the coding work I do most often, Zed has become a fast, comfortable option on Windows.

5 developer tools that are incredible even if you're not a developer

Powerful tools built for developers, useful for everyone

3
By  Yash Patel

RustDesk

Remote access without the cloud

Sometimes I need to access another Windows machine without physically sitting in front of it. Instead of relying on a cloud-based remote desktop service, I started using RustDesk for those situations. It gives me a straightforward way to connect to another computer and work with its desktop remotely.

What I like most is that I can use it when I need to quickly check something on another machine, access a file, or troubleshoot an issue. The interface is simple enough that I don't have to spend much time figuring out how to start a remote session.

RustDesk also fits my preference for open-source, self-hosted software. I can run my own server components when I want more control over how the connection is managed instead of depending entirely on a third-party service.

I don't open it every day, but when I need remote access, having a tool I can control and rely on makes the process much easier.

Bruno

A cleaner way to test APIs

When I work with APIs, I don't want to keep recreating the same requests or rely on a browser tab every time I test something. Bruno gives me a dedicated place to create, save, and run my API requests while keeping everything close to my development projects.

I can create requests for different endpoints, add headers and parameters, send request bodies, and quickly check the response. What I find particularly useful is keeping related requests together in collections. That makes it easier to return to an API I worked with earlier without rebuilding everything from scratch.

Bruno also fits nicely into my local-first workflow because my collections can stay on my machine instead of being tied to a hosted account. I can keep them alongside a project and manage them like other development files.

It has become a simple part of my API workflow, especially when I'm testing endpoints repeatedly during development and want my requests organized and ready to run.

These underrated tools handle everything around my actual coding.

A better workflow doesn't need more complexity

I’ve found that a productive Windows development setup doesn’t have to be complicated. The right open-source tools can quietly improve the way I work without forcing me to completely change my habits. What matters most is finding software that solves the small problems I regularly run into. These tools have done exactly that for me, making my everyday development workflow feel simpler, faster, and more comfortable.

item.title: SATA SSDs are still the smartest second drive you can buy, and I can't justify spending more on NVMe
item.itunes:title: SATA SSDs are still the smartest second drive you can buy, and I can't justify spending more on NVMe
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Talking about a SATA SSD in 2026 is anathema to many PC users. It's akin to recommending a console to a PC building enthusiast. I fully expect people to bring up the outdated performance and needless cables of SATA SSDs when I still recommend it as a secondary drive. NVMe SSDs are faster, sleeker, and more convenient, and I would always use them for the primary drive, but SATA SSDs aren't outdated by any means.

Most PC users don't need NVMe read/write speeds for the bulk of what they do on their systems. Spending more on NVMe drives in this market won't make a tangible difference to your day-to-day experience, except for a few workloads that most people never touch. Moreover, some users may not even have the option of installing a second NVMe SSD, making SATA the only choice.

Your next SSD might be SATA again — here's why that's not a problem

The market forces have made SATA SSDs relevant again

By  Tanveer Singh

Most of what you do on your PC doesn't need NVMe speeds

The SATA to NVMe transition hasn't benefited the average user

It's tempting to do a repeat and get a second NVMe SSD (Gen4 or Gen5) for your PC. Even a Gen4 drive is nearly 13 times faster than a SATA SSD, and all that extra throughput would surely go somewhere, right? After using an NVMe SSD as your primary drive for years, you're probably not willing to entertain the notion that a SATA SSD is still more than enough for your workloads.

The reality is, however, that most people don't need 7,000 MB/s or 15,000 MB/s read/write speeds for their PC to feel snappy. NVMe drives are in a different league when it comes to large file transfers and productivity workloads like video editing and database processing. That said, these sequential speeds don't really matter for what you probably do on your PC every day — gaming, browsing, working, and restarting the PC a few times.

OS boot times and game loading times are storage-dependent, but once you've moved from a hard drive to a SATA SSD, there's little room for improvement. And regular system navigation and launching applications is no sweat for a SATA SSD. Adding a second NVMe drive might seem simpler, but there's another aspect to it.

I paid for a PCIe 5.0 SSD, and my games load exactly as fast as they did on my old drive

It definitely isn't worth the $100 premium, at least for now.

15
By  Hamlin Rozario

Buying a SATA SSD is cheaper in this terrible market

The lesser of two evils

There was a time when the price difference between a SATA and NVMe SSD for the same capacity was non-existent. Then, the "AI-powered" DRAM shortage hit the globe a year ago, and everything changed. Within a few months, SSD prices saw a four-fold increase, and NVMe drives were the worst hit. A year later, things aren't looking much different, but as it stands, SATA SSDs are indeed cheaper than equivalent NVMe options.

You don't need to look beyond Amazon to see this in action. Popular 1TB NVMe Gen4 drives are going for around $170, whereas 1TB SATA drives are sitting at "just" $130. That's a 23% discount for virtually the same experience. This disparity grows as you compare larger SATA and NVMe drives, strengthening the case for the former.

No one knows if prices will ever come back to pre-2026 levels. If you need additional storage right now, buying a SATA SSD makes sense from both financial and performance standpoints. The value for money is just not there for NVMe drives, unless you're a professional or power user who can actually make use of blazing-fast transfer speeds.

I bought the cheap SSD instead of the fastest one, and I'd do it again

My storage is abundant and my wallet is happier for it

5
By  Abhinav Raj

Buying SATA is way simpler for older systems

When you run out of M.2 slots

There's another angle to this NVMe vs. SATA comparison, especially for people with older motherboards. It's possible that your old motherboard has a single M.2 slot, which is already occupied by your primary NVMe SSD. Dual M.2 slots became common on budget and mainstream motherboards only around 5–6 years ago, before which a single M.2 slot was fairly common.

On such systems, adding a second NVMe drive isn't feasible, making a SATA SSD the only choice. Moreover, the PCIe lane-sharing situation on older motherboards might make it complicated to introduce additional M.2 slots using PCIe adapters. Doing so can deprive your SATA ports or other expansion slots of PCIe bandwidth, so it's a whole different consideration.

In contrast to M.2 slots, even older motherboards had ample SATA slots to accommodate additional hard drives or SATA SSDs. If responsive secondary storage is all you need, a 1TB SATA SSD is the smartest choice on an older PC.

I tried using an M.2 SSD in a PCIe adapter instead of my motherboard, and the results were impressive

Add more speedy storage with those unused slots.

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Buying SATA over NVMe is the smarter choice in 2026

It's no secret that PC hardware prices have exploded across components. From RAM and SSDs to GPUs, nearly everything is wildly overpriced due to enterprise demand. In this market, SATA SSDs are the ideal pick for secondary storage, even on a gaming PC. Unless you're a professional or heavy productivity user, you don't really need the performance of Gen4/Gen5 NVMe SSDs.

item.title: This single package manager replaced WinGet, Homebrew, and APT on all my computers
item.itunes:title: This single package manager replaced WinGet, Homebrew, and APT on all my computers
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most people tend to install apps on their computer using the obvious methods: you may find apps on an app store, or download an installation file directly in the browser. But if you read XDA, you probably already know about package managers and how much more convenient they can be.

The problem is package managers aren't always the most intuitive. They often require you to use the terminal, which requires different commands depending on your platform. And in some cases, like Linux, you may even need multiple package managers.

That's where UniGetUI comes in, and it's a game-changer.

It started on Windows

A package manager to rule them all

I've written about UniGetUI a couple of times before, but when I did, I was coming at it from the perspective of a Windows user, because that's where the project started, and arguably where it's still the most useful.

UniGetUI for Windows brings together all kinds of package managers, starting with Microsoft's own Winget, along with Chocolatey and Scoop. This is a pretty big deal because there are valid reasons for all these package managers to exist and be used. Chocolatey and Scoop both predate Winget, and it's not hard to understand why some might still prefer to use them over a solution that's controlled by Microsoft.

By bringing all these options together, not only can you choose your preferred method for installing apps and do so without using terminal commands that can be confusing, but you can also combine these to cover any apps that aren't in a specific package manager. Winget may have a lot, but there are some more obscure packages that are still only available on Chocolatey and Scoop.

5 Reasons UniGetUI is the best package manager for Windows

If you want the easiest way to install you favorite apps and utilities, UniGetUI is the best package manager you can use.

3
By  Brian Burgess

On top of that, of course, UniGetUI also integrates package managers for more specific tools. It support Npm, Pip, Bun, PowerShell Gallery, and more, which all serve very specific purposes for power users and developers. Just about any package manager you use on your system can be managed through UniGetUI, including a search engine that searches across all package managers at once (with filtering options) and a centralized update interface.

For Windows users, I've recommended UniGetUI for a few years now.

There are benefits on Linux, too

And yes, it's distro-aware

The spirit of UniGetUI is still alive and well if you decide to use it on a Linux PC, and it works exactly how you'd expect if you transposed its Windows functionality to Linux. The more dedicated package managers, like Npm, Cargo, and PowerShell Gallery (for the cross-platform PowerShell) are still here, and it's the more general package managers that differ.

UniGetUI on Linux supports both Flatpak and Snap, the two primary "universal" package managers that work on just about every Linux distro. You can search for apps and get updates automatically from these two systems, along with Homebrew, if you've set it up.

But what about native package managers? Well, UniGetUI is also distro-aware, meaning it will support the package manager your distro uses, but there seems to be a big caveat to that. I tested this on both Ubuntu-based distros (AnduinOS, specifically) and Arch, but while UniGetUI can search and install new packages from these managers, it's not able to search for updates in them.

Oddly, if you search for updates in the terminal, you can then see the available updates in UniGetUI and install them that way, but if you're opening the terminal anyway, the point of UniGetUI is kind of lost. I'm not sure if this is a design limitation or a bug in the current release, but it does reduce the usefulness of the app. Still, I love it for the ability to search and update the other kinds of packages available.

Linux package managers are the main reason I'll never switch back to Windows, ever

You'll have to pry them out my CLI.

37
By  Rich Edmonds

Macs get the least goodies

But it's useful all the same

Finally, macOS also has its own version of UniGetUI, and as you might expect, it's technically where the app has the fewest capabilities. Though, despite that, it's still pretty useful.

This is because macOS doesn't really have a package manager that's very widely used for all kinds of apps. The only two ways to install apps on a Mac are using the App Store or downloading an installer file from the web; there isn't a centralized update system otherwise. That means there's no way a package manager can handle all your apps.

Homebrew is just as good on Linux as it is on Mac

This tool works just as well on Linux as it does on macOS, offering consistent workflows, user-space installs, and cross-platform simplicity.

1
By  Jeff Butts

Still, I've found UniGetUI very useful on my Mac Mini because it supports Homebrew. While it's not meant for full-blown apps, Homebrew is a great package manager for all kinds of tools I (and many others) rely on, such as ffmpeg for transcoding video or yt-dlp for downloading videos from YouTube. Most of the time, these tools go months without getting updates on my PC because I never bother to open the terminal and check, so UniGetUI brings those updates to my attention and makes them much easier to install.

Plus, other package managers like Pip and Npm are also still supported on macOS, so there are still plenty of use cases to consider here.

It gives me control and flexibility

Manage updates, create bundles, and more

Aside from the package management aspect in itself, UniGetUI also has a few features that are universal across the three platforms it's available on. In addition to finding apps and checking for updates, UniGetUI provides additional controls for them. When you install a package, you can set it to ignore all future updates. Or, later on, you can pause updates for a given package, if you're aware of a known issue, for example.

Another cool feature of UniGetUI that I love is being able to create bundles of packages, which you can then install in one fell swoop. Because you have multiple package managers in one, you can create bundles of packages across all of them. What's more, for package managers like Pip or Npm, which are supported on multiple platforms, you can even create bundles on Linux and use them on a Mac, for example. It's a unifying solution in more than one way.

UniGetUI deserves more appreciation

I've long loved what UniGetUI does for Windows PCs, but after discovering that it's now a multi-platform tool, I admire it even more. I do wish the Linux implementation was more complete, but otherwise, this is an excellent way to bring package updates under one roof so I can make sure my system is always up-to-date.

UniGetUI

item.title: Snap Layouts wasn't built for ultrawide monitors, so I built my own with PowerToys
item.itunes:title: Snap Layouts wasn't built for ultrawide monitors, so I built my own with PowerToys
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've used the Alienware AW3423DW OLED for the last four years, and though I bought it for gaming, I now mostly use it as a secondary monitor that gives me plenty of room to multitask. That 21:9 aspect ratio gives me extra width to keep multiple windows open side by side without making any of them feel too cramped. And since I'm usually juggling Discord, Chrome, and TradingView, even while gaming, Snap Layouts were a no-brainer for quickly organizing everything.

Now, as much as I've enjoyed using Snap Layouts since Windows 11 first launched, I've always found the preset layouts a little too restrictive for an ultrawide monitor. Even though Microsoft says the layouts you see may depend on display size, my ultrawide doesn't get anything particularly special compared to my other two 16:9 monitors. That's what convinced me to try out FancyZones in Microsoft PowerToys when I first read about it, and after seeing how much more customizable it is, I haven't looked back.

4 Windows 11 tiling managers that put Microsoft’s Snap Layouts to shame

Upgrade your productivity

1
By  João Carrasqueira

FancyZones lets me build the layout I want

And I can have a different layout for each of my three monitors

If you just use FancyZones as it is after installing PowerToys, you're going to be disappointed because you only have like five preset layouts to choose from. Snap Layouts, on the other hand, gives me eight on each monitor. So, to take full advantage of it, you need to create a custom layout by going to PowerToys Settings -> FancyZones -> Open layout editor. Since my main issue with Snap Layouts was that it didn't give me a layout to arrange four windows horizontally, that's exactly what I created.

I split my ultrawide into four equal zones, and now I can fit four windows side by side without having to manually resize each one afterward. You can go crazy with the layouts, but I just wanted something practical. My favorite part about FancyZones is that it remembers which layout I've assigned to each monitor. For my 4K monitor, I created the same four-window grid that I'm used to with Snap Layouts, and for my other standard 1440p one, I created a simple two-column layout. This way, each of my three monitors has a layout that actually suits how I use it.

FancyZones gets the snapping part right

I don't have to drag windows all the way to the edges

For a feature called "Snap Layouts," you'd expect the actual snapping process to be its biggest strength. Except it's only straightforward when you're snapping windows to the edges or corners of your screen. To see more layout options, you need to drag a window all the way to the top edge of your monitor. And then you still have to drop the window into the zone you want. Of course, you can hover over the maximize button instead, but even that's near the top-right corner, so you're still mostly moving your cursor across the screen just to bring up the layouts.

With FancyZones, I just hold Shift while dragging a window, and my custom zones immediately show up. Then I can drop the window into whichever zone I want without dragging it to the top edge of my screen first. This might not seem like a big deal, but on a 34-inch ultrawide, it saves me a lot of mouse movement when I'm constantly rearranging windows. And since I already know where each zone is, I don't have to stop and think about where I want to put the window every time.

Snap Layouts has simplicity going for it, though

But FancyZones is mostly a one-time setup that only takes a few minutes

If there's one thing Snap Layouts gets right, it's that you don't have to set anything up. If you like the predefined layouts, you don't need to mess around with anything else. And if you just want a simple split-screen or four windows arranged in a grid, you don't even need to bring up the layouts in the first place. The layout you want to use can change depending on what you're doing, too, and Snap Layouts makes it easy to switch between them on the fly. With FancyZones, it's not nearly as straightforward until you set it up properly.

But you only need to set it up the way you like once. For instance, you can create multiple custom layouts and assign a number to each of them. After that, you can switch between them any time by pressing Win + Ctrl + Alt + [number]. The keybind is kind of ridiculous, but I've rarely found myself needing to switch layouts on my ultrawide anyway. And I can still use Snap Layouts when I want a different arrangement. So I can basically use whichever one makes more sense at the time, depending on whether I'm holding that Shift key when I drag a window around.

Snap Layouts needs more customization to win me back

I don't think it should be hard for Microsoft to add a few more layout options to Snap Layouts. Even something as simple as letting me arrange four windows horizontally would solve my biggest problem with it on an ultrawide. But ideally, I'd like to see Microsoft go a step further and let me create my own layouts. And the whole snapping process could use some work, too. After using FancyZones, I now prefer holding another key to have my zones appear while dragging a window. Maybe one day we'll get that flexibility in Snap Layouts, but until then, I'm keeping FancyZones enabled alongside the other PowerToys utilities I now use every day.

That 21:9 aspect ratio gives me extra width to keep multiple windows open side by side without making any of them feel too cramped. And since I'm usually juggling Discord, Chrome, and TradingView, even while gaming, Snap Layouts were a no-brainer for quickly organizing everything.

Now, as much as I've enjoyed using Snap Layouts since Windows 11 first launched, I've always found the preset layouts a little too restrictive for an ultrawide monitor. Even though Microsoft says the layouts you see may depend on display size, my ultrawide doesn't get anything particularly special compared to my other two 16:9 monitors. That's what convinced me to try out FancyZones in Microsoft PowerToys when I first read about it, and after seeing how much more customizable it is, I haven't looked back.

Upgrade your productivity

FancyZones lets me build the layout I want

And I can have a different layout for each of my three monitors

So, to take full advantage of it, you need to create a custom layout by going to PowerToys Settings -> FancyZones -> Open layout editor. Since my main issue with Snap Layouts was that it didn't give me a layout to arrange four windows horizontally, that's exactly what I created.

I split my ultrawide into four equal zones, and now I can fit four windows side by side without having to manually resize each one afterward. You can go crazy with the layouts, but I just wanted something practical. My favorite part about FancyZones is that it remembers which layout I've assigned to each monitor. For my 4K monitor, I created the same four-window grid that I'm used to with Snap Layouts, and for my other standard 1440p one, I created a simple two-column layout. I don't have to drag windows all the way to the edges

item.title: Flathub just reversed its AI-generated content ban, but developers still need to say they used it
item.itunes:title: Flathub just reversed its AI-generated content ban, but developers still need to say they used it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Flathub now allows AI-generated code if disclosed and labeled with the affected parts and extent.
  • Submitters must be human; agents can't generate commits, descriptions, reviews, or replies.
  • Maintainers can still reject AI-labeled or fully vibe-coded apps if they are low quality or problematic.

Back in May of this year, we reported that Flathub banned AI-generated submissions because people were being a little rude about it.

Now, as more and more Linux distros have declared acceptance of LLM-created code (as long as it's of high quality, of course), it seems that Flathub has had a change of heart. Fortunately, while the new rules allow AI content if it's properly disclosed, they don't open the door for people to flood the repository with poorly made apps.

Flathub now allows AI-generated apps, but they still have to be good

People can't get out of submitting bad apps just because they said an AI made it

As spotted by Linuxiac, Flathub has gone back on its ban on LLM-created content. Now, in a revised commit to the documentation, the rules begin as follows:

Submitters must disclose any AI-generated code, documentation, packaging, or other material they know or reasonably believe is included in the application or its Flathub packaging. The disclosure must identify the affected parts and approximate extent.

This doesn't mean someone can tell an LLM to make an app in five minutes, slap a disclosure on it, submit it, and earn immunity from being taken off Flathub. If the maintainers believe a project was entirely vibe-coded, or they have "concerns about its review, quality,

or maintainability," they can reject an app even if the submitter correctly labeled their work. It seems like a push to encourage AI tools without opening the door to a tidal wave of vibe-coded apps that overwhelm maintainers.

On top of that, people cannot just spin up an AI agent and have it maintain their project for them. Humans must submit the work themselves, and an agent cannot "generate their commit messages, descriptions, review comments, or replies." This is likely to stop people from parking an agent on a project and having it do all the maintenance work.

Linus Torvalds used AI to fix a Linux bug, and now LLM critics on Linux face an uncomfortable choice

Avoiding software without AI code is getting very difficult.

item.title: The most useful productivity tool I installed this year costs nothing and does one thing perfectly
item.itunes:title: The most useful productivity tool I installed this year costs nothing and does one thing perfectly
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve installed plenty of productivity apps over the years, and most of them promise to help me work faster, stay organized, or save time. This year, though, the app that made the biggest difference was one I almost overlooked. It isn’t a task manager, note-taking app, or AI assistant. It’s a small Windows utility that sits quietly in the background and solves a problem I didn’t realize was slowing me down. After using it regularly, I started wondering how something this simple had become one of the most useful tools in my workflow.

Windows clipboard history wasn’t enough

I needed more from my clipboard

Windows' built-in clipboard history was useful, but I kept hitting its limits. I could press Win + V and see a few recent items, which was enough for basic tasks. But as my work became more detailed, I noticed how quickly that history became hard to use.

As a blogger, I constantly copy snippets, links, headings, quotes, search terms, and bits of text while researching and writing. I often need something I copied several minutes ago, not necessarily the last thing I copied. Windows clipboard history made that harder than it needed to be because I had to scroll through the list and visually look for the right item.

I also had a simple problem with how I worked. I rarely copy something just once. I might copy a sentence, switch to another window, copy a URL, grab another piece of text, and then realize I need the first sentence again. At that point, the clipboard started feeling less like a useful history and more like a temporary holding area.

I didn't need another complicated productivity system. I just wanted my clipboard to remember more of what I had copied and make those items easier to reuse. That's when I started looking beyond Windows' built-in option.

Ditto changed everything

My most underrated productivity tool

I tried multiple clipboard managers before settling on Ditto, and most of them either felt too complicated or added features I didn’t really need. Ditto was different. It was simple enough to get out of my way, but capable enough to become genuinely useful in my daily workflow.

After installing it, I didn’t need much time to figure out how I wanted to use it. I kept working as usual and slowly started relying on it whenever I needed something I had copied earlier. That made a bigger difference than I expected.

I started using it while researching articles, moving information between different windows, and collecting small pieces of text that I knew I would need again. Instead of interrupting what I was doing to save something somewhere else, I could leave it in my clipboard history and keep going.

That sounds like a tiny improvement, but I noticed the difference almost immediately. I was spending less time recopying things and less time wondering where I had put a piece of text.

After trying several options, Ditto was the first clipboard manager that felt like it belonged on my PC rather than another app I had installed just to test.

The boring features are my favorites

The small things that matter

Once I started using it regularly, I began appreciating how much control it gives me over something as simple as copied content. One feature I use often is searching my clipboard history. When I know I copied something earlier but can’t remember exactly when, I don’t have to keep scrolling and guessing. I can search for a word or phrase and quickly find what I need. For my research-heavy work, that is genuinely useful.

Keyboard shortcuts are another reason Ditto feels so natural to me. Instead of reaching for the mouse every time I want to access my clipboard, I can open Ditto with a shortcut, move through my history, and select what I need. It sounds minor, but when I’m constantly switching between my browser, editor, and other apps, those few seconds add up.

I also like being able to pin items that I use repeatedly. Things like common phrases or text snippets can stay available instead of getting buried among newer copies. None of these features sound exciting on their own. That’s probably why I like them. They solve small problems without trying to turn the clipboard into an entire productivity system.

I tried replacing default Windows clipboard with 4 open source tools, and only one stuck

Windows gave me Win + V; I went looking for something better and found a clear favorite.

By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, the smallest tools make the biggest difference

I used to think productivity apps needed to solve big problems to be worth keeping. Ditto changed that perspective for me. It doesn’t try to organize my entire life or add another system to maintain. It simply makes one everyday part of working on Windows less frustrating. That’s probably why I’m a little embarrassed to call a clipboard manager my productivity app of the year. But after using it regularly, I can’t imagine going back to working without it.

Ditto

Ditto is a simple clipboard manager for Windows that adds a lot more functionality, including the ability to remember copied files and retain items indefinitely.

Instead of reaching for the mouse every time I want to access my clipboard, I can open Ditto with a shortcut, move through my history, and select what I need. It sounds minor, but when I’m constantly switching between my browser, editor, and other apps, those few seconds add up.

I also like being able to pin items that I use repeatedly. Things like common phrases or text snippets can stay available instead of getting buried among newer copies. None of these features sound exciting on their own. That’s probably why I like them. They solve small problems without trying to turn the clipboard into an entire productivity system.

I tried replacing default Windows clipboard with 4 open source tools, and only one stuck

Windows gave me Win + V; I went looking for something better and found a clear favorite.

By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, the smallest tools make the biggest difference

I used to think productivity apps needed to solve big problems to be worth keeping. Ditto changed that perspective for me. It doesn’t try to organize my entire life or add another system to maintain. It simply makes one everyday part of working on Windows less frustrating. That’s probably why I’m a little embarrassed to call a clipboard manager my productivity app of the year. But after using it regularly, I can’t imagine going back to working without it.

Ditto

Ditto is a simple clipboard manager for Windows that adds a lot more functionality, including the ability to remember copied files and retain items indefinitely.

item.itunes:title: AMD squeezed a lightweight FSR 4 model onto handhelds, but older devices might miss out
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • AMD will bring a lightweight FSR 4 to APUs, gaming laptops, and handhelds by the end of the year (pre‑2027).
  • Lightweight FSR 4 could fit older handhelds, but AMD hasn't confirmed updates to existing devices.
  • AMD will expand FSR 4 across existing APUs and new product lines; exact rollout details remain unclear.

Back when AMD brought FSR 4 to GPUs (including retroactively adding it to older models), AMD said it was a little skeptical about squeezing the same tech onto handhelds. It never explicitly stated it would never bring FSR 4 to devices such as handhelds, but it never outright confirmed that it would, either.

Now, AMD has announced a new lightweight version of FSR 4 for handheld APUs, and while it sounds like the tech may now be small enough to fit on older handhelds, we still don't know for sure if AMD can, or will, bring the tech to existing handhelds.

AMD's FSR 4 will arrive on "APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices" before 2027

It may just be new models that will get it, though

As spotted by The Verge, South Korean publications such as TheElec reported that Jack Huynh, the Senior Vice President and General Manager of AMD’s Computing and Graphics Group, spoke at Seoul Dragon City in Yongsan. During the meeting, Huynh said the following (machine-translated from Korean):

"We will expand the machine learning AI-based FSR4 technology, which was first introduced to existing external graphics cards, to the entire product line, including APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices, by the end of this year. We plan to respond in two directions: launching existing APUs and new product lines."

To achieve this, AMD will release a lightweight version of FSR 4 designed to run off APUs. But if the company is going that far, could it add FSR 4 to older hardware, as it did with GPUs? Unfortunately, Huynh neither confirmed nor denied this would happen; just that we'll see something before 2027 comes around. Maybe it's only for new devices, or maybe not; either way, we've reached out to AMD for context, so stay tuned.
